Practical

What helps today

In shortAdd what the boring task is missing. Stuck right now? Start with the "Try one thing" picker just below; evidence badges show how well each idea is supported.

When a task stalls

Stuck? Try one thing.

Three steps, about a minute. You don't need to read anything else first.

  1. 1

    What's true about the task?

    Find the line below that fits best.

  2. 2

    Do this one thing now.

    Pick an answer in step 1 and one idea appears here.

    If it's boring

    • Put on a playlist you only play for this task.
    • Move somewhere new: another room, a café, outside.
    • Start with a question you'd like answered, then go find out.

    If you can't start

    • Do only the first tiny step, like opening the file. You can stop after that.
    • Walk briskly for 10 minutes, then sit straight down and begin.
    • Pick one of two tasks. Choosing is enough to get moving.

    If it never ends

    • Work for 15 minutes on a timer, then stop. That counts.
    • Count what you finish: emails sent, pages read, boxes packed.
    • Set a small finish line, like "just the top shelf".

    If you dread it

    • Say why it matters to you: "I file taxes so I can book the trip."
    • Pair it with a treat you only get while doing it.
    • Tell someone when you'll be done, then start.

    If you're not sure

    • Start a 10-minute timer and do only the first tiny step.
    • Tell someone what you're about to do, then start.

  3. 3

    Did you start within 10 minutes?

    Yes: use the same idea next time. No: try another one. That isn't failing. It's how you find what works for you.

Must-do task with a deadline? Tell someone when you'll be done, then start the timer. The deadline gets you going, and your reason keeps you going.

Why these work, and how strong the evidence is

Each idea adds something the stalled task is missing. These come from the catalyst research. They are ideas to try, not proven treatments.

  • Urgency (timers, telling someone) Plausible
  • Movement (a brisk walk first) Good, general population
  • Visible progress (counts, finish lines) Modest
  • Pleasure (a playlist or treat kept for the task) Modest; fades
  • Novelty (a new place or tool) Lab evidence only
  • Curiosity (start with a question) Lab evidence only
  • Choice (pick one of two) Plausible, untested
  • Your reason (link it to something you want) Plausible, untested

Ideas lose their pull as they become familiar, so swap to a new one every week or two.

Keep it healthy: skip ideas that cost you sleep, and don't lean on extra caffeine, which hasn't been shown to help ADHD. Ignore "dopamine hack" and "dopamine detox" claims, which have no evidence behind them.

Quick tips

The same principle that drives the research works in daily life, with or without a diagnosis: add what the boring task is missing. Body doubling and treat bundling now sit with the workflows below. Most of the evidence comes from ADHD studies. Evidence levels are shown so you can judge for yourself.

Strong evidence

If you have ADHD, ask about medication

Stimulants measurably increase how rewarding a task feels. For diagnosed ADHD they are among the most effective treatments studied in psychiatry.

Good evidence, not yet in adult ADHD

Make starting tiny

Commit only to the first step ("open the document"). Set things up the night before. Use "when X happens, I do Y" plans, which work in the general population but haven't been tested in adults with ADHD.

Plausible

Create urgency with someone else

Work in 15–25 minute timeboxes, and tell a person when you'll be done. Many people find this helps them start. The evidence is thin: the best-known study on deadlines was retracted in 2026, and timers and deadlines have not been tested in people with ADHD. Try it and keep it if it works for you.

Moderate

Move first

A short burst of exercise before a demanding task gives a small-to-moderate boost to focus and self-control.

Modest

Reward the comeback

After a missed day, give yourself a small reward for getting back on track. It was the best of 54 strategies in a large gym study.

Small, unblinded studies

Try white or pink noise

Background noise gave a small benefit in ADHD and a small cost for people without ADHD. Studies so far weren't blinded.

Plausible

Make time visible

Use a visual timer, see time as space on a calendar, or set gentle vibration reminders.

Plausible

Keep it fresh

Rotate where and how you work. Race your last time. Novelty fades, so keep rotating.

Plausible

Show one next task

Hide the full list. Let a person, a rule, or an app choose the single next thing so you don't have to compare.

Supplements

Supplements are popular, but most have small or inconsistent effects on ADHD and none replaces evidence-based treatment. Several help mainly when a person is actually deficient, so a blood test is the sensible first step. The same evidence badges apply.

Early, not tested in ADHD

Zinc glycinate for sleep

Zinc plays a role in sleep regulation, and most of a handful of small trials outside ADHD found zinc improved adults' self-rated sleep quality, though not diagnosed sleep disorders. No trial has tested it for sleep in ADHD. One small study found the glycinate form better absorbed than zinc gluconate. Keep total zinc, from food and supplements, under 40 mg a day; more, long term, can cause copper deficiency.

Only if deficient; very limited evidence

Iron

Children with ADHD have lower iron stores (ferritin) on average. The only treatment trial was a small pilot in 23 children with low ferritin, with mixed results, and no adult trial exists. There is no reason to take it if levels are normal. Get tested first, and keep iron tablets away from young children, as overdose is dangerous.

Little or no benefit

Omega-3 fish oil

The largest review (Cochrane, 2023, 37 trials) found no effect on ADHD symptoms, and UK guidelines (NICE) advise against it for ADHD. Some analyses hint at a small benefit in longer trials or in children with low omega-3 levels, but these are unconfirmed.

Small, add-on only

Vitamin D

Four small trials in children taking stimulant medication found a small extra benefit from adding vitamin D, with low-certainty evidence. There are no adult trials. Correcting a deficiency is worthwhile for general health anyway.

Small, mixed

Broad micronutrient formulas

In a well-run 8-week trial in unmedicated children with ADHD and irritability, more children on micronutrients were rated much improved overall (54% versus 18%), but parent-rated ADHD symptoms did not improve more than placebo. One adult trial of a commercial formula found self-rated but not clinician-rated improvement.

Small, low-quality studies

Zinc and magnesium for focus

Six small trials in children found zinc improved overall ADHD scores, but not attention or hyperactivity on their own, with low-certainty evidence. Magnesium levels are slightly lower in ADHD, but it has mostly been tested in combination products.

Small, low-quality studies

Saffron

A few small trials in children, mostly from one country, compared it with stimulant medication in one trial and added it to medication in others. No trial has tested saffron alone against placebo, and results need independent replication.

Not shown to help ADHD

Caffeine

It briefly increases alertness, but pooled trials in children with ADHD found no clear benefit over placebo, and medication worked better in a head-to-head trial. It can worsen sleep and anxiety and adds to the stimulant effects of ADHD medication.

Tested; no clear benefit

St John's wort and ginkgo

St John's wort did no better than placebo in a controlled trial in children, and it interacts with many medicines, including antidepressants and birth control pills. Ginkgo worked far less well than medication in one trial and gave a modest, unreplicated boost when added to it in another.

Supplements are not reviewed for effectiveness before sale, and quality varies between brands. Some interact with ADHD medication or other drugs. Check with a doctor or pharmacist before starting one, especially when pregnant or taking other medication.

Also worth checking: sleep and body-clock timing, mood, anxiety, thyroid, iron levels, and for women, menstrual-cycle and perimenopause changes. Treating these can make a large difference, whatever the diagnosis.

Things to explore

Workflows for dull but important tasks

In shortSix practical ways to get the focus of a deadline without the panic, each matched to a kind of dull task, with honest evidence ratings.

Cramming works for many people because a close deadline wakes the brain up. These workflows try to get the same lift without the last-minute panic. Each one is a practical version of an engagement ingredient this program plans to test.

The "interest-based nervous system"

A popular clinical idea, associated with psychiatrist William Dodson, holds that people with ADHD engage through five triggers (interest, novelty, challenge, urgency, and passion) rather than importance. It fits what research finds about task-dependent focus. But it is a clinical description, not a tested theory, and the same pattern appears to a lesser degree in people without ADHD. That is why the program measures it as a dimension rather than treating it as a separate kind of brain.

Why cramming works, and what it costs

A close deadline raises arousal, driven largely by noradrenaline, into the range where focus comes easily. A matching rise in dopamine is plausible but has not been measured. Cramming also has costs: for anything that must be remembered, spreading work out beats last-minute effort, and the stress adds up. The workflows below try to keep the lift and drop the panic.

Six workflows to try

Popular, untested

Body doubling

Ingredient tested: social presence

Example
You can't clean a room or write a report alone, but you finish easily when a friend sits quietly nearby or on a silent video call.
Why it may work
Another person's presence adds light accountability and raises alertness. Research on working in front of others finds it helps with simple, familiar tasks but can hurt with hard, new ones.
Try it
Book a 45-minute virtual co-working session, or sit in a busy café, just for paperwork, expenses, or inbox triage. Save new, difficult work for quieter settings.
Plausible, untested in ADHD

Beat-the-clock micro-sprints

Ingredients tested: urgency and challenge

Example
Racing to unload the dishwasher before the microwave timer ends, or cleaning the whole apartment in 20 minutes because guests are on the way.
Why it may work
A tight, arbitrary limit turns a long, boring task into a short game with a score, and leaves no time for perfectionism.
Try it
Set a strict 15-minute timer and process as many routine emails, invoices, or forms as you can. Track the count like a high score, stop when the timer ends, and take a 5-minute break.
Modest; fades

Temptation bundling

Ingredient tested: immediate reward

Example
Only watching a favorite show while folding laundry or walking on a treadmill.
Why it may work
Dull tasks pay off only at the end. Pairing them with something enjoyable that you allow yourself only during the task adds a reward you feel right away. In larger studies the effect was smaller and faded over time.
Try it
Keep a gripping audiobook, a high-energy playlist, or a favorite drink only for bookkeeping, filing, or data entry. Swap the treat when it stops working.
Good evidence, not yet in adult ADHD

Zero-friction staging

Ingredient tested: size of the first step

Example
Leaving running shoes in front of the bedroom door, so going for a run needs no setup decisions.
Why it may work
Getting started is often the hardest point. Every small step before the real work (finding a password, opening a folder, clearing the desk) is another chance to stall. Removing setup steps and planning "when X, I do Y" both help in the general population.
Try it
Set up the starting point the night before: leave the tax spreadsheet open, put the mail on the keyboard, or draft email templates for recurring messages.
Untested; use with care

Productive procrastination

Ingredient tested: task switching

Example
Deep-cleaning the kitchen at 11 p.m. to avoid writing one difficult email.
Why it may work
Avoiding a hard task often comes with restless energy. Steering it onto useful small jobs clears backlogs. The risk is that the relief of avoiding the main task makes avoiding it again more likely, and its deadline still slips.
Try it
Keep a short menu of small chores, such as booking appointments, paying bills, or renewing subscriptions. When you stall on the main project, do two items, then go straight back to the main task.
Good evidence, not yet in adult ADHD

Write down the exact next action

Ingredient tested: size of the first step

Example
Sticking the grocery list to your keys instead of keeping it in your head.
Why it may work
Working memory is reliably weaker in ADHD, and holding a multi-step task in mind is tiring. Writing down the first physical action removes the guesswork.
Try it
Replace "Handle insurance paperwork" with "Open portal, download PDF statement, save to Desktop."

Matching the workflow to the task

Different dull tasks stall for different reasons. This matrix is a starting hypothesis, and the program plans to test whether matching the workflow to the bottleneck beats using one workflow for everything.

Task typeMain bottleneckWorkflow to tryRule of thumb
Admin and paperworkTaxes, forms, billingNo novelty; many setup stepsBody doubling + zero-friction stagingOpen every portal and tab first, then finish it in a live 50-minute co-working block.
Routine upkeepInbox, filing, organizingEndless scope; no finish lineBeat-the-clock micro-sprintsSet a 12-minute countdown and clear as many items as you can before it ends.
Repetitive workData entry, compliance reviewUnder-stimulation; mind wanderingTemptation bundlingUse headphones with a playlist or podcast kept only for this work.
Errands and follow-upsCalls, renewals, schedulingHard to startProductive procrastinationKeep a visible 3-item list and do one as a "break" when deep work stalls.

Start now

A three-step checklist

  1. Pick one stalled task that has sat on your list for more than two days.
  2. Shrink the first step to one physical action, and do the setup now: open the exact web page, or put the document in front of your keyboard.
  3. Add one constraint to your next work block: a hard 15-minute timer, an audio treat kept for this task, or a 30-minute co-working session.

None of these workflows has been tested as a package in adults with ADHD. The Engagement Transplant Study tests their ingredients one by one and in combination, including whether the benefit lasts once the extra support stops.

Not medical advice. This site describes a research approach and summarizes published evidence for general education. It does not diagnose or treat any condition, and nothing here is a reason to start, stop, or change a medicine or supplement. Talk to a qualified clinician about assessment or treatment.

Struggling right now? In the US, call or text 988. In the UK and Ireland, call Samaritans on 116 123. Elsewhere, find a free helpline at findahelpline.com. In an emergency, call your local emergency number.
